```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(ranger)
library(patchwork)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
set.seed(123)
```

## Failure leaves signatures

Everything so far in this section has described fitting as a search. A search can fail, and
the useful thing about failure is that it leaves signatures. This page is about recognising
them.

The reason to care is that a failed fit does not usually look like a failed fit. It returns
coefficients. It prints a summary. It makes predictions. Section 3 contained one model that
produced a perfectly respectable ROC AUC while predicting presence at zero stations, and the
optimisation there was working exactly as instructed, which is precisely why you cannot rely
on output looking reasonable.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The idea

Three things can go wrong between asking for a fit and getting one:

1. **The search did not finish.** It ran out of iterations and returned wherever it had
   reached.
2. **The search finished somewhere arbitrary.** The objective had several minima and the
   starting point chose between them.
3. **The search finished nowhere.** The objective has no minimum in the direction the
   algorithm was heading, and it kept going until a limit stopped it.

Each has a recognisable fingerprint, and all three are demonstrated below on this survey.

## Worked example

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

d <- survey |>
  select(abundance, present, catch_weight_kg, depth_m, temperature_c,
         chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season) |>
  drop_na()
```

### Failure 1: the search did not finish

Iterative fits stop either because they converged or because they hit a cap. These are
completely different outcomes and the printed coefficients look the same.

```{r}
#| label: maxit
#| warning: true
stopped_early <- glm(present ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m, data = d,
                     family = binomial, control = glm.control(maxit = 2))

full_fit <- glm(present ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m, data = d, family = binomial)

tibble(
  fit        = c("maxit = 2", "run to convergence"),
  converged  = c(stopped_early$converged, full_fit$converged),
  iterations = c(stopped_early$iter, full_fit$iter),
  chlorophyll = c(coef(stopped_early)[2], coef(full_fit)[2]),
  depth       = c(coef(stopped_early)[3], coef(full_fit)[3])
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

The truncated fit reports a chlorophyll coefficient of −0.312 against the correct −0.344:
9% out, and entirely plausible-looking on its own. The only thing distinguishing them is
`$converged`, which is a field you have to ask for.

The habit worth forming: **after any iterative fit, check the convergence flag rather than
the coefficients.** For `glm()` it is `fit$converged`. For `glm.nb()` it is a warning. For
`nnet` and `glmnet` it is in the object. Under tidymodels, `extract_fit_engine()` gets you
to it.

### Failure 2: the search finished nowhere

This one produces the most memorable output in applied statistics. `catch_weight_kg` is the
leaked column from [section 2](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd), computed
from `abundance`, so it separates present from absent almost perfectly.

```{r}
#| label: separation
#| warning: true
separated <- glm(present ~ catch_weight_kg, data = d, family = binomial)

round(summary(separated)$coefficients, 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: separation-flags
c(converged = separated$converged, iterations = separated$iter)
```

A coefficient of −157.7 with a standard error of 13,515 and a *p*-value of 0.99. Read that
plainly: the model has found a predictor that classifies the response essentially perfectly,
and reports it as the least significant variable you have ever seen.

Both numbers are correct and neither is meaningful. When one predictor separates the classes,
the likelihood has no maximum: pushing the coefficient further from zero always makes the
data slightly more probable, forever. The algorithm walks off in that direction until it hits
its iteration cap at 25, and the standard error, being the curvature of a surface that is
flattening out towards infinity, goes to infinity with it.

::: {.callout-warning}
**A gigantic coefficient with a gigantic standard error is not weak evidence. It is a
separation warning.** The clue is the ratio: an estimate of 158 with an error of 13,515 is
not an estimate at all. If you see this, look for a predictor that encodes the answer, which
in real work usually means [leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd), as it does
here. R does print `fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred`, and it is one of the
few warnings that always means something.
:::

### Failure 3: the search finished somewhere arbitrary

Not every algorithm lands in the same place twice. Random forests choose bootstrap samples
and variable subsets at random, so an unseeded fit is a different model each time.

```{r}
#| label: ranger-runs
set.seed(1)
split <- initial_split(d |> select(-present, -catch_weight_kg), prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

unseeded <- map_dbl(1:5, \(i) {
  forest <- ranger(abundance ~ ., data = train, num.trees = 500)
  sqrt(mean((test$abundance - predict(forest, test)$predictions)^2))
})

round(unseeded, 4)
```

Five runs, five answers, spanning 0.037 RMSE. That is small, and it is the point. Section 3's
[ten-model comparison](../03-supervised-learning/choosing-a-method.qmd) separated several
models by less than that, which is exactly why that page refused to treat small gaps in the
table as a ranking. **Run-to-run noise is a measurement you can make, and it sets the
resolution of every comparison you go on to draw.**

For k-means the same instability is much larger, because the objective genuinely has multiple
minima:

```{r}
#| label: kmeans-starts
X <- scale(d |> select(depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu))

single_starts <- map_dbl(1:20, \(i) kmeans(X, centers = 5, nstart = 1, iter.max = 50)$tot.withinss)

tibble(
  `distinct solutions found` = n_distinct(round(single_starts, 3)),
  best  = min(single_starts),
  worst = max(single_starts),
  `with nstart = 25` = kmeans(X, centers = 5, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1)))
```

Twenty runs of the same algorithm on the same data found ten different answers, the worst 5%
worse than the best. Every one of them converged. This is the difference between the convex
objectives of [regression](parameter-estimation.qmd), with one minimum always found, and
objectives that are merely bumpy, and it is why
[section 8](../08-unsupervised-learning/index.qmd) insists on `nstart`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-instability
#| fig-cap: "Run-to-run variation from two algorithms with no seed set. The random forest's test RMSE varies over a narrow band; k-means' objective across twenty single random starts takes ten distinct values spanning 5%. Both algorithms reported success every time."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of dot strips. The upper panel shows five random-forest test RMSE values clustered between 4.72 and 4.76, a span of under 0.04. The lower panel shows twenty k-means objective values scattered between 1094 and 1152, clumping at several distinct levels rather than spreading evenly, with a marked point at the lowest value labelled as the solution found with twenty-five restarts."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
p1 <- tibble(value = unseeded) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, 0)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) +
  labs(x = "Test RMSE (individuals)", y = NULL,
       title = "Random forest, 5 unseeded runs") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

p2 <- tibble(value = single_starts) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, 0)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) +
  annotate("point", x = min(single_starts), y = 0, shape = 1,
           size = 6, stroke = 1, colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Total within-cluster sum of squares", y = NULL,
       title = "k-means, 20 single random starts",
       subtitle = "Circled: the value nstart = 25 also finds") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

p1 / p2
```

## Three failures, three responses

The three failures need three different responses.

| Signature | What happened | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `converged = FALSE`, or a `maxit` warning | Ran out of iterations | Raise the cap; if it still fails, the model is wrong for the data |
| Huge coefficient, huge standard error, *p* ≈ 1 | Separation: no maximum exists | Find the predictor that encodes the answer; suspect leakage |
| Different answer each run | Stochastic algorithm, possibly multiple minima | Set a seed for reproducibility; measure the spread to know your resolution |
| `NaN` loss, or coefficients exploding | Learning rate above the stable limit | Lower it; [scale the predictors](gradient-descent.qmd) |
| Coefficients change wildly on small data changes | Flat valley, near-collinearity | Check correlations; consider [a prior](map-and-priors.qmd) |

Two of these deserve emphasis because they are routinely misread.

**Setting a seed makes a fit reproducible. It does not make it stable.** A seeded random
forest returns the same number every time, which is necessary for a reproducible paper and
tells you nothing about whether that number is reliable. The way to find out is to remove the
seed deliberately and run it several times, as above. Reproducibility and stability are
different properties and only one of them is about your science.

**Warnings are not all equal.** `fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred` always
means something. So does `algorithm did not converge`. By contrast, the rank-deficiency and
`NA` coefficients that `lm()` produces from collinear predictors arrive with no warning at
all: R simply drops a term and prints `NA` in the table, and nothing tells you it happened.
The loud messages are not a reliable guide to the dangerous failures.

### A checklist

After fitting any model in this course, before reading a single coefficient:

1. Did it converge? Not "did it print output": check the flag.
2. Are any coefficients absurd in size, or are any `NA`?
3. Is any standard error orders of magnitude larger than its estimate?
4. If the algorithm is stochastic, what does it do on a second run without a seed?
5. Are the predictions in a possible range, with no negative counts, no probabilities outside
   (0, 1), nothing outside what the species can do?

Item 5 catches more real mistakes than the other four combined, and it needs no statistics at
all.

## Limits of these checks

**A converged fit can still be the wrong model.** Everything on this page is about whether the
optimisation did what it was asked. It cannot tell you whether you asked for the right thing.
A Poisson model on overdispersed counts converges beautifully;
[section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd) is about that second question.

**Convergence tolerances are set by package authors, not by you.** "Converged" means "changed
by less than some default on the last iteration", and defaults vary between packages fitting
the same model. Two packages can disagree in the third decimal and both report success.

**Some failures have no signature at all.** Section 2's
[stratified split](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) silently ignored the stratification
variable, produced a worse balance than not stratifying, and issued no warning of any kind.
No checklist would have caught it. Only checking that the result was what you asked for did.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- Check the **convergence flag**, not the plausibility of the coefficients. A fit stopped
  after two iterations here was 9% out and looked entirely normal.
- A huge coefficient with a huge standard error and *p* ≈ 1 means **separation**, not weak
  evidence: here, a coefficient of −158 with an error of 13,515 from a leaked predictor.
- Stochastic algorithms give a different answer per run: the forest varied by 0.037 RMSE,
  k-means found ten distinct solutions out of twenty runs.
- **Seeding gives reproducibility, not stability.** Remove the seed on purpose to measure how
  much your result moves, and treat that spread as the resolution of your comparisons.
- The warnings that print loudest are not the failures most likely to mislead you.

:::

## Try it yourself

1. Fit `glm(present ~ abundance, family = binomial)` on this data. `present` is defined as
   `abundance > 0`, so the separation is exact. Compare the coefficient and standard error to
   the `catch_weight_kg` version: which is worse, and why does that ordering make sense?
2. Run the k-means block with `centers = 2` instead of 5. Does the number of distinct solutions
   go up or down, and what does that suggest about the relationship between model complexity
   and the number of places an algorithm can get stuck?
